newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vital Albania elections set to go ahead.
newsitem.headline: Vital Albania elections set to go ahead.

text.p: Elections regarded as vital to prevent Albania sliding back into chaos and anarchy were back on track on Thursday as the country's second-largest party agreed to take part.

Agreement by the Socialist Party to run in the June 29 vote, provided there is full monitoring of the vote by the international community, ends months of deadlock and lifted a last obstacle to the elections going ahead.

"We took a political decision which represents a responsible attitude of the Socialist Party to take part only in guaranteed free, democratic and fair elections," Socialist Party chairman Fatos Nano told reporters.
"The Socialist Party will only take part in elections that have an international guarantee they will be free, fair and equal," the party said in a statement.
Other parties in premier Bashkim Fino's nine-party government, all much smaller than the Socialista and Democrats, have not yet said whether they will stand in the vote.
However European envoy Franz Vranitzky said in Vienna earlier that Fino had called him the previous night and assured him the parties had agreed to take part in the election.
Albania needs the election to restore law and order after riots and looting in March sparked by the collapse of shady investment schemes that left many penniless in Europe's poorest country.
The Socialists and other parties had refused to stand over electoral rules they said were tilted in favour of right-wing President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party.
The Socialists, reformed heirs of the Communist Party that ruled this mountainous state with an iron fist for more than 40 years, are the main rivals to the Democratic Party.
A Socialist official said the party would check continuously during the campaign to make sure the election was fair.

Fino, a Socialist who leads a national unity government installed as the riots reached a peak, asked the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on Wednesday for "Bosnia-style" monitoring.
The Socialists pulled out of elections in May 1996, saying they were rigged. The OSCE called them seriously flawed.
The Socialists said they wanted the OSCE, the Council of Europe and the European Union to be involved at every step of the election right up the final count.
Vranitsky, special OSCE envoy to Albania, earlier reassurned the Balkan nation of wide-ranging international support for the election.
He said that as many observers as necessary would be sent by the OSCE and the Council of Europe.

"We will help Albania. The whole international community is speaking with unanimity. There are no dissenting voices," Vranitzky told a news conference after addressing the OSCE's Vienna-based permanent council.
One politician said Albania needed the same kind of all-embracing monitoring of its election as in Bosnia.
Albania is much calmer than at the height of the violence in March, but several regions are still tense and large swathes of the country are without any state control.
Gangs armed during the wholesale looting of army barracks, when around one million weapons fell into civilian hands, appear to roam free and police are absent from many areas.
The international community had sent a barrage of warnings to Albania, saying aid and assistance for the might be withdrawn unless the elections went ahead.
